blocks.title: Classification of Carbohydrates
blocks.text:
• Monosaccharides (Simple Sugars): Glucose, Fructose, Galactose
  • Oligosaccharides:(2 to 10 Monosaccharides): Maltose, Sucrose, Lactose
  • Polysaccharides (Many Monosaccharides): Starch, Cellulose, Glycogen

blocks.title: Reducing Sugar
blocks.text:
It possesses a free aldehyde or ketone group, which is essential for their reducing properties.

Example:- Glucose, Fructose, Galactose, Maltose, Lactose

blocks.title: Non-reducing Sugar
blocks.text:
No free aldehyde or ketone group: The aldehyde or ketone groups are involved in the formation of glycosidic bonds, leaving no free groups to react with oxidizing agents.

Example;-  Sucrose, Starch, Cellulose, Glycogen

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following is a reducing sugar?

a) Sucrose

b) Maltose

c) Starch

d) Cellulose
blocks.answer:
Answer: (b) Maltose

Explanation:

  • Reducing sugars are carbohydrates with a free aldehyde or ketone group capable of reducing                                                      $Cu^{2+}Reducing Sugar (RCHOH)\rightarrow\ {Oxidized Sugar}(RCOOH) + Cu_2O$ in Benedict's or Fehling's test.
  • Maltose has a free hemiacetal group, allowing it to act as a reducing sugar.
  • Sucrose lacks a free hemiacetal group due to glycosidic linkage.
  • Starch and cellulose are polysaccharides without free-reducing groups.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Which of the following is a monosaccharide?

a) Starch

b) Cellulose

c) Glucose

d) Sucrose
blocks.answer:
Answer: (c) Glucose

Explanation:

  • Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates that cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller sugar units.
  • Glucose is a monosaccharide with the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$.
  • Starch and Cellulose are polysaccharides (made of multiple glucose units).
  • Sucrose is a disaccharide (composed of glucose and fructose).

blocks.title: Anomer's And Epimer's
blocks.text:
• Anomer's : Differ in configuration at 1st carbon due to hemi (acetal or ketal) ring formation. The new-asymmetric carbon is referred to as Anomeric carbon.

Eg α−D. Glucose and β−D. Glucose

• Epimer's : Diastereomer's which differ in configuration at any one chiral carbon

eg:

• D-Glucose & D-mannose
    • D-Glucose & D-Galactose

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following pair of sugars are anomers?

a) Glucose and fructose

b) α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose

c) Glucose and galactose

d) Mannose and glucose
blocks.answer:
Answer: (b) α-D-glucose and β-D-glucose

Explanation:

  • Anomers are isomers of a sugar that differ in configuration only at the anomeric carbon (the carbon derived from the carbonyl group during cyclization).
  • In α-D-glucose, the hydroxyl group on the anomeric carbon is below the plane of the ring, while in β-D-glucose, it is above.
  • Glucose and fructose are not anomers; they are structural isomers.
  • Glucose and galactose, and mannose and glucose, differ in configurations at carbons other than the anomeric carbon, making them epimers, not anomers.

blocks.title: Invert Sugar
blocks.text: Sucrose(which is dextrorotatory) is known as invert sugar because upon hydrolysis it breaks down into Fructose (laevorotatory) and Glucose (dextrorotatory). The specific rotation value of Fructose is more than glucose due to which the mixture overall is laevorotatory. So, basically dextrorotatory sucrose converts to laevorotatory mixture on hydrolysis (inversion of optical activity) and hence is called invert sugar.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The bond that links two monosaccharides in a disaccharide is called?

a) Peptide bond

b) Glycosidic bond

c) Ester bond

d) Phosphodiester bond
blocks.answer:
Answer: (b) Glycosidic bond

A glycosidic bond is the covalent bond that links two monosaccharides by a condensation reaction, involving the removal of a water molecule.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Which of the following disaccharides is a reducing sugar?

a) Sucrose

b) Maltose

c) Lactose

d) Both b and c
blocks.answer:
Answer: (d) Both b and c

  • Reducing sugars have a free aldehyde, Hemiacetal, ketonic and, hemiketal group. The sugar is oxidized in carboxylic acid  and copper ($C{u^{ + 2}}$) is reduced into $C{u^{ + 1}}$
$C{u^{ + 2}} + R - CHO \to RCOOH + C{u^{ + 1}}orC{u_2}O$

+2                   oxidation                             +1

Reduction

  • Maltose and Lactose are reducing sugars because they have a free anomeric carbon in one of their monosaccharide units.
  • Sucrose is not a reducing sugar because its anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond, leaving no free-reducing group.

Sucrose is a disaccharide made up of one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose joined by a glycosidic bond.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Polysaccharides Carbohydrates which yield a large number of monosaccharide units on hydrolysis are called
polysaccharides. Some common examples are starch, cellulose, glycogen, etc. Polysaccharides are not
sweet in taste, hence they are also called non-sugars.
The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars.

Examples of polysaccharides: Starch, Cellulose, Glycogen

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Amino acids are organic molecules that serve as the building blocks of proteins.

They contain an amino group ($-NH_2$), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom, and a side chain (R group)

blocks.title: Structure
blocks.text:
A central carbon atom (α-carbon) bonded to:

• An amino group (-$NH_2$)

• A carboxyl group (-COOH)
    • A hydrogen atom
    • A side chain (R group)

blocks.title: Classification of Amino Acids
blocks.text:
• Based on R group properties:
  • Nonpolar, hydrophobic amino acids: Alanine, Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Proline, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, Methionine.
  • Polar, hydrophilic amino acids: Serine, Threonine, Cysteine, Tyrosine, Asparagine, Glutamine.
  • Charged amino acids:
  • Acidic: Aspartic acid, Glutamic acid
  • Basic: Lysine, Arginine, Histidine

blocks.title: Properties of amino acids
blocks.text:
• They are typically white or colorless crystalline substances.
  • Amphoteric: Can act as both acids and bases.
  • Zwitterionic: Exist as both positively and negatively charged ions.
  • Optical Activity: except glycine Most amino acids are chiral.

blocks.title: Peptide Bond Formation
blocks.text:
• A covalent bond formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another amino acid.
  • Water is released as a byproduct.

blocks.title: Protein Structure
blocks.text:
• Primary Structure: The linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain.
  • Secondary Structure: The local folding of the polypeptide chain, stabilized by hydrogen bonds:
  • α-helix: A helical structure.
  • β-pleated sheet: A sheet-like structure.
  • Tertiary Structure: The overall three-dimensional shape of a polypeptide chain, stabilized by various interactions (hydrogen bonds, disulfide bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions).
  • Quaternary Structure: The arrangement of multiple polypeptide chains to form a functional protein.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
The bond formed between two amino acids is called a?

a) Glycosidic bond

b) Phosphodiester bond

c) Peptide bond

d) Hydrogen bond
blocks.answer:
Answer: (c) Peptide bond

A peptide bond is a covalent bond formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another, resulting in the release of a water molecule.
blocks.prompt:
The bond formed between two amino acids is called a?

a) Glycosidic bond

b) Phosphodiester bond

c) Peptide bond

d) Hydrogen bond

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
The secondary structure of a protein is stabilized by?

a) Disulfide bonds

b) Hydrogen bonds

c) Ionic bonds

d) Hydrophobic interactions
blocks.answer:
Answer: (b) Hydrogen bonds

The secondary structure of a protein, such as alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, is primarily stabilized by hydrogen bonds between the backbone atoms of the polypeptide chain.

d) Hydrophobic interactions

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question:
Which of the following is NOT an essential amino acid?

a) Lysine

b) Leucine

c) Glycine

d) Valine
blocks.answer:
Answer: (c) Glycine

Glycine is a non-essential amino acid, meaning the body can synthesize it.
Lysine, Leucine, and Valine are essential amino acids, which must be obtained through the diet because the body cannot produce them.
